messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: UX Designer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 73

He sits in his office, the glow of two monitors cutting through the early morning dark. On one screen, a wireframe of a health-tracking app; on the other, a browser tab with his lab results from last week—all normal now. He scrolls up and down anyway, three times, before closing the tab for the third time that hour. Then he checks his pulse at the wrist. Steady. He does this every fifteen minutes, sometimes more.

Two years ago, he was at his desk—a different desk, a different apartment—when a sharp, crushing pressure bloomed behind his sternum. He remembers the ceiling tiles in the emergency room, counting them to stay calm. The doctors said viral myocarditis. They said young, healthy men survive this. He was in the ICU for eleven days. He remembers the beeping, the cold of the IV line, the way his wife’s hand trembled in his. He remembers the moment a junior resident said “cardiac arrest” in the hallway outside his door, not realizing he could hear. It was a different patient. But that word never left him.

Now he cannot walk past a hospital without his breath shortening. He takes the long way to avoid the one on his commute. When a colleague mentions a cold, he steps back. His desk is scrubbed clean each morning—alcohol wipes, then bleach, then alcohol again. He knows it’s irrational. He still does it.

At night, he lies awake next to his wife, listening to his own heartbeat. If it skips—even the benign kind everyone has—he jolts upright, certain this is the one. The last time he woke her to take him to the ER, the EKG was normal. The attending asked if he was under stress. He said no. He was a UX designer. His job was to make things functional, frictionless. He hated friction. Now every sensation in his body is friction.

His work has changed. He used to prototype health apps with enthusiasm, believing in behavior change. Now he avoids those projects. His manager noticed, and he offered a story about needing creative variety. He now designs a travel app instead. But even that trickles with triggers: hotel rooms remind him of the hospital bed; flight insurance reminds him of mortality. He spends hours on pixel alignment, redoing micro-interactions twelve times. The perfectionism keeps the thoughts at bay, but it exhausts him. His team says he’s a stickler. They don’t know he’s running from his own body.

His wife asks him about the distance. She is patient, but he sees her sadness. They used to cook together; now he eats separate food—no salt, no sugar, no risk. He cannot explain why a single grain of sodium feels like a death sentence. He says he’s just being healthy.

On weekends, he walks in a park near their home. He keeps a mental map of every bench and defibrillator location, just in case. He has never used one. He rehearses the steps in his head.

This morning, after closing the lab results tab for the final time, he opens his design software. The cursor blinks. His hands are still. He feels the pulse in his temples, the thrum of life that should be a comfort but is only a warning. He tells himself: *I am fine. I survived.* But survival, he has learned, is its own kind of illness. He takes a breath and begins to trace the outline of a button. He will make it round, soft, familiar. He will call it “Next.” He will never press it.
